messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Alvarez, a 36-year-old married tax consultant, came to treatment after years of trying to keep himself functioning by keeping his world narrow and controlled. He described a deployment in which a routine patrol changed in an instant when an improvised blast struck the vehicle ahead of his unit. In the blast’s aftermath, what stayed with him most was not only the sight and sound of the explosion but the bitter, metallic taste in his mouth as he dragged himself through smoke and dust, tasting grit and blood while trying to understand who was still alive. In the first months afterward, certain conversation topics—anything about military losses, injuries, or “what happened over there”—could make his mind snap back to that scene. When the memory came, he said it could hit with such force that he had to stop mid-sentence, overwhelmed by emotion, or else he would feel strangely numb, as if the event belonged to someone else. He had come to dread those returns of memory because they did not arrive as distant recollections; they arrived with the taste, the emotion, and the blunt sense that danger was present again.  

Daniel’s reactions shaped the way he moved through ordinary life. He avoided talking with anyone about the event or its aftermath, and he also pushed away positive feelings when they surfaced, because they felt unsafe and almost naive in the face of what he knew could happen. After a few painful attempts at opening up with his wife, he began changing the subject whenever she asked about his service, and he noticed that even a well-meaning touch on the shoulder could make him recoil. Any form of physical contact with others became something he braced against, and this withdrawal had a quiet but steady effect on his daily life: at home he sat farther from his wife on the couch, and at work he kept his interactions clipped and professional, avoiding casual warmth that might invite more than he could manage. At the same time, these habits made the event feel even less integrated into his own life. Because he refused to speak about it and worked hard not to feel anything good or soft, the memory remained sealed off, returning in fragments rather than in a fuller narrative. When it did return, it often did so through a cue that seemed trivial to others—a certain topic raised in conversation, or the sudden physical sensation of being touched unexpectedly—and the more he shut himself down, the more stark and unbidden those recalls became.  

Over time, Daniel became increasingly watchful. Unusual silence made him feel something dangerous was about to happen, and he would scan a room for exits before he could settle enough to stay. That habit was especially obvious in his office and at client dinners, where he sat with his back to the wall and mentally identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere. A quiet conference room, a lull in conversation, or a colleague stepping too close could all make his body react as if the threat were immediate. He startled with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly, and that alarm was not random: it was rooted in the way his memory could flare up without warning, carrying the taste of the event and the old certainty that disaster could erupt from calm. In turn, the more he organized his life around avoiding touch, avoiding conversation, and dodging any rush of positive feeling, the less room he allowed for reminders to settle into context. The remembered scene returned in more stripped-down form—sometimes vivid enough that he could taste it again, sometimes numbed out and unreal—and each recurrence made him more alert for danger in the present. He began reading silence as a sign of imminent harm, and he became quicker to notice potential triggers in other people’s words, their tone, or the way they reached toward him.  

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the narrowing of his life. What brought him in was a recent evening at home when his wife touched his arm in the darkened kitchen and he jerked away hard enough to frighten her, then later found himself overwhelmed by a sudden rush of the memory when a dinner conversation turned to old service stories. He hated that the event could still command him so completely, and he was most afraid that if he kept backing away from contact, from conversation, and from any feeling that seemed too good to trust, he would end up living as if the blast had never ended. At the same time, he hoped that treatment might help him face the memory without being overtaken by it, and make ordinary closeness with his wife and the rest of his life feel safe again.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers bringing back the memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers themselves cause or drive the memory to occur within a paragraph.
The vignette describes the memory leading to triggered reactions, but it does not explicitly convey that the memory itself causes or generates triggers.
The vignette shows threat increasing vigilance and alarm, but it does not clearly state that threat leads to specific triggers or triggering cues.
The vignette shows maladaptive strategies affecting his life and making the event less integrated, but it does not clearly state that these strategies lead to the memory returning.
